nodes.label: Dong et al. (2021) studied 9 women with primary infertility from 7 independent families. The first was a pedigree in which 2 sisters had recurrent hydatidiform moles. The other 7 patients from 6 families had embryonic arrest or recurrent implantation failure, found by screening patients with embryonic arrest, recurrent implantation failure, or recurrent pregnancy loss.

Dong et al. (2021) used whole-exome sequencing, with confirmation by Sanger sequencing, to identify 5 novel biallelic MEI1 mutations in 9 infertile women from 7 families. Two novel mutations were found in the pedigree with 2 sisters who had recurrent hydatidiform moles. Three further novel mutations were found in 7 patients from 6 families with embryonic arrest or recurrent implantation failure.

In in vitro studies by Dong et al. (2021), protein-truncating and missense MEI1 mutations reduced MEI1 protein levels on western blot. In minigene assays, splicing mutations caused abnormal alternative splicing of MEI1.
Wu et al. (2024) reported a female infertile patient with embryonic arrest and recurrent implantation failure.

In a female patient with embryonic arrest and recurrent implantation failure, Wu et al. (2024) used whole-exome sequencing, with Sanger sequencing confirmation, to identify compound heterozygous frameshift variants in the MEI1 gene (NM_152513.3): c.3002delC and c.2264_2268+11delGTGAGGTATGGACCAC. Each variant was inherited from a heterozygous parent, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

Wu et al. (2024) found that 2 day-3 cleavage-stage embryos and 2 day-6 blastocysts from the MEI1-mutant patient were all aneuploid, with numerous monosomies and trisomies, on whole-genome sequencing and whole-genome bisulfite sequencing. Global methylation levels in the 2 blastocysts were 0.344 and 0.168, far outside the optimal window of 0.25 to 0.27. The authors suggested that the genetic makeup of arrested embryos may help explain why MEI1 mutations cause either embryonic arrest or monospermic androgenetic hydatidiform moles.

Liu et al. (2025) studied a consanguineous family with an infertile female patient whose embryos arrested and an infertile male patient with azoospermia. Preimplantation genetic testing showed high rates of chromosomal abnormalities in the arrested embryos.

In the 2 affected members of a consanguineous family, a woman with embryonic arrest and a man with azoospermia, Liu et al. (2025) found a homozygous deletion of all of exon 19 of the MEI1 gene. They identified it by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed it by Sanger sequencing. cDNA sequencing confirmed that the exon was missing from the transcript, and quantitative expression analysis found almost no MEI1 exon 19 expression in the patients. The patients' mother was a heterozygous carrier. In transfected HEK293T cells, Western blotting showed a truncated MEI1 protein, consistent with the predicted premature termination in exon 20.

nodes.label: Liu et al. (2025) suggested that aneuploidy in embryos carrying the MEI1 mutation may explain their reduced developmental potential and their arrest.

Jiao et al. (2025) described a 32-year-old Chinese woman (F1_II:4) with a 4-year history of primary infertility, regular menses and normal ovarian reserve. Her husband's semen and both partners' karyotypes were normal. Of 22 mature oocytes, the 8 fertilized by ICSI became 3PN or PPN embryos. With conventional IVF, 5 oocytes formed normal 2PN embryos and 3 became 3PN/PPN embryos. All 2PN-derived embryos failed to form blastocysts, whereas 2 of 3 3PN/PPN-derived embryos from ICSI developed into late-stage blastocysts.
Formation of multiple pronuclei during fertilization

Jiao et al. (2025) described a 35-year-old Chinese woman (F2_II:2) with an 8-year history of primary infertility, regular menses, normal ovarian function and patent fallopian tubes. She had 2 unsuccessful IVF cycles and then 1 ICSI cycle. In the ICSI cycle, 3 oocytes formed 2PN embryos and 1 formed a 1PN embryo. All embryos failed to form blastocysts, and transfer of 2 frozen embryos did not result in pregnancy.

Jiao et al. (2025) performed whole-exome sequencing in 20 women who had a high rate of abnormal fertilization during ICSI at a center in Guangzhou, China. Biallelic MEI1 variants were found in 2 of the 20 women, and all 4 variants were novel.

In the proband of family 1, Jiao et al. (2025) identified compound heterozygous MEI1 variants by whole-exome sequencing, confirmed by Sanger sequencing: c.622T-C (p.Ser208Pro) in exon 6 and c.2647C-T (p.Arg883Ter) in exon 21. The p.Ser208Pro missense variant was absent from gnomAD and was classified as of uncertain significance. In HEK293T cells it did not alter MEI1 protein expression. The p.Arg883Ter nonsense variant had a gnomAD frequency of 6.57E-06. It increased MEI1 mRNA but reduced MEI1 protein levels, which the authors considered consistent with nonsense-mediated decay.

In the proband of family 2, Jiao et al. (2025) identified compound heterozygous MEI1 variants: a c.3037T-G (p.Trp1013Gly) missense variant in exon 24 and a deletion of exons 21 to 31. The deletion is reported as c.2546_3525del in the text and as c.2546_3825del in the table and discussion. Because the deletion spans c.3037, the patient appeared homozygous for c.3037T-G, and qPCR validated the copy-number loss. The missense variant was absent from gnomAD and increased MEI1 protein levels in HEK293T cells, whereas the deletion did not alter protein expression.

Jiao et al. (2025) performed whole-genome sequencing and parental-contamination testing on 3 embryos from the family 1 proband. All 3 embryos were triploid with an excess of maternal chromosomes, including an embryo that had appeared to be a normal 2PN embryo. Haplotype analysis indicated that the triploidy was of meiotic origin: meiosis II errors in the 3PN zygote and meiosis I errors in the 3PN blastocyst and the 2PN blastomere. The authors proposed that the MEI1 variants impair meiosis I through abnormal chromosome synapsis.

Jiao et al. (2025) performed RNA-seq on 3 day-3 embryos from the family 1 proband and compared them with control embryos. They found 2,005 downregulated and 1,904 upregulated genes. Downregulated genes were enriched for meiotic cell cycle and epigenetic regulators, including histone demethylases and deacetylases. Maternal-effect genes were dysregulated, and qPCR confirmed reduced MEI1, MKI67, ASTL and WEE2 expression. The authors suggested a dual mechanism of impaired meiotic and mitotic cell cycles and genomic stability, together with dysregulated epigenetic processes that disrupt zygotic genome activation.

Jiao et al. (2025) summarized reported MEI1 variants and observed that those associated with nonobstructive azoospermia tended to lie toward the N terminus, whereas variants associated with embryonic developmental arrest tended to cluster toward the C terminus. They stated that this hypothesis requires further validation.

Jiao et al. (2025) recommended screening for MEI1 variants in patients with abnormal fertilization patterns, especially multiple pronuclei after ICSI. They noted that even 2PN embryos that look morphologically normal may be triploid. They also suggested that 3PN/PPN blastocysts might implant and could develop into hydatidiform moles in natural pregnancies.

Chen et al. (2026) studied female patients with primary infertility characterized by early embryonic arrest (EEA) and implantation failure, including affected women from 2 unrelated families carrying biallelic MEI1 variants.

In affected women from 2 unrelated families with female infertility due to early embryonic arrest and implantation failure, Chen et al. (2026) identified biallelic MEI1 variants by whole-exome sequencing, confirmed by Sanger sequencing: a novel homozygous variant in one family and compound heterozygous variants in the other. Bioinformatics analysis indicated the variants were rare and possibly deleterious.

In HEK293T cells transfected with wildtype and mutant constructs, Chen et al. (2026) found that the MEI1 variants did not alter the subcellular localization of MEI1 but significantly affected its mRNA and protein expression levels, potentially leading to impaired protein function.
